title: When a Busy Team Is Over-Managed and Under-Led
summary: A team can hit every sprint and still drift. John Kotter's split between management and leadership, how to spot the gap, and small habits that bring direction back.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Monday standup, 9:30. Everyone has an update. Three tickets moved to in review, two PRs merged over the weekend, the dashboard is green and the call ends two minutes early. Now catch one person on the way out and ask: "What are we trying to get done this quarter, and why does it matter?" You'll probably get a pause, then a careful sentence about the current sprint.

Nothing is broken here. The work is planned, tracked and shipped. What's missing is harder to see on a board: a shared answer to where all this work is heading. John Kotter had a name for that state back in 1990, when he wrote that most US corporations were "overmanaged and underled." Plenty of engineering teams fit the description today.

Two jobs, not two rungs on a ladder

Kotter's article What Leaders Really Do (first published in Harvard Business Review in 1990, reprinted in 2001) draws the line in two sentences: "Management is about coping with complexity. Leadership, by contrast, is about coping with change." He then breaks each one into three parts. Translated into engineering terms, it looks like this:

Management: coping with complexity Leadership: coping with change
Kotter's three parts Planning and budgeting; organizing and staffing; controlling and problem solving Setting a direction; aligning people; motivating and inspiring them
On an engineering team Roadmaps and estimates, team setup and hiring, sprint tracking, incident follow-ups Deciding what the product should become, getting everyone to pull the same way, keeping people going when the plan shifts
Questions it answers How will we build it? When will it be done? What are we trying to change? Why does it matter?
When it's the only one you have Steady shipping with no destination Big plans that never ship

Here's the part people tend to skip: Kotter doesn't rank them. "Strong leadership with weak management is no better, and is sometimes actually worse, than the reverse." A team that's all vision and no follow-through burns out on plans that never land. A team that's all process and no direction keeps shipping, neatly, in a circle. You need both, often from the same person on the same day.

A full board and an empty horizon

An over-managed, under-led team is hard to spot because it looks healthy. Everyone's busy, every ticket has an owner, velocity holds steady. From the inside, being busy and having a direction feel exactly the same.

The easiest way to hear the gap is to notice which questions get asked. A team can have sharp answers to how and when while nobody has said a clear sentence about what and why in months. A few signs worth watching for:

  • Sprint goals are lists of tickets. Take out the ticket numbers and there's nothing left to say.
  • Trade-offs get settled by whatever is easiest this sprint, because nobody can name a bigger goal to check against.
  • Ask "why are we building this?" and people quote whoever requested it.
  • Retros talk about process (standup length, Jira columns) and almost never about whether the work changed anything for users.
  • Strong engineers stay productive but stop proposing things.

Why teams drift toward managing

This rarely happens because managers are lazy. Management is simply the safer move under pressure. How and when are measurable, urgent and closeable. You can move a ticket, update an estimate and end the day with a tidier board. That feels like doing your job, and partly it is.

What and why are none of those things. They're fuzzy, slow and a bit uncomfortable, and they rarely close inside one sprint. So when a deadline gets close, you reach for the lever that visibly moves (control) and put off the one that asks you to sit with uncertainty. It's the difference between tidying your desk and deciding what the desk is for. Tidying gives you a hit of progress right away. Deciding looks a lot like staring out the window at 4 p.m. on a Thursday.

What leading looks like on an ordinary Tuesday

It's easy to picture leadership as a big moment: an all-hands, a memorable speech, a slide with a mountain on it. That picture gets in the way, because no ordinary Tuesday ever feels big enough to count.

In practice it's small and repetitive. In Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail, Kotter lists "undercommunicating the vision by a factor of ten" among the classic mistakes. Treat the ten as a rule of thumb. Kotter didn't measure it. The point holds: you'll be bored of the why long before most of the team has really heard it. So good leads repeat it in small places, like the first two minutes of planning, the way a task gets framed, or a straight one-line answer to "why are we even doing this?"

Google's research on its own managers shows the two jobs sitting in one role. Project Oxygen drew on more than 10,000 data points from performance reviews and feedback surveys, plus interview notes, to work out what effective managers do. Its list of ten behaviors puts "implement a clear vision and strategy" right next to "empower the team without micromanaging" and "focus on productivity and results" (re:Work, Following the data).

The other half of leading is clearing away what stops people from moving: the fear of being wrong in front of everyone, of breaking something, of asking a question that shows you were lost. None of that is one visible event. It builds up the way trust or a healthy codebase does, one small conversation at a time, until the direction shows up in how the team talks about its own work.

A small way to rebalance

You don't need a reorg to start fixing this. A handful of habits will do.

  • Three to one. In planning or a 1:1, for roughly every three how-or-when questions, ask one what-or-why. It's a habit to build. Don't track it as a metric.
  • Put the destination where people look: a pinned message, the top of the board, the first line of the sprint goal. A strategy deck nobody reopens doesn't count.
  • Write the why into the ticket. One line on who it helps and how you'll know it worked.
  • Ask them to tell you. Every few weeks, instead of explaining why the work matters, ask a teammate to explain it to you. If they can't, don't file it as a performance problem. You've just found the spot where the direction went missing.

How it looks at different altitudes

This isn't only a manager's problem. As an individual contributor, you lead every time you tie your part of the work to the bigger why: in a PR description, in how you frame a trade-off, in the question you raise when the room would rather move on. As a tech lead or engineering manager, more of your week tilts toward what and why. Dropping how and when entirely is its own failure, and that's the next post in this series, Vision Without Craft. The higher you go, the more the risk flips: a leader so far above the details that the vision stops touching anything real.

Try this week

  • In your next planning meeting, ask one "why" for every three "how" or "when" questions.
  • Write this quarter's goal as one sentence and pin it where the team looks every day.
  • Pick one ticket in progress and add a line about who it helps.
  • In one 1:1, ask your teammate why their current work matters. Hear the whole answer before you add anything.

faqs.q: What is the difference between leadership and management?
faqs.a: In John Kotter's 1990 Harvard Business Review article "What Leaders Really Do", management is coping with complexity: planning and budgeting, organizing and staffing, controlling and problem solving. Leadership is coping with change: setting a direction, aligning people and motivating them. A team needs both at the same time.

faqs.q: Can the same person be both a leader and a manager?
faqs.a: Yes, and most tech leads switch between the two many times a day. Google's Project Oxygen research lists "implement a clear vision and strategy" and "focus on productivity and results" as behaviors of the same effective managers. The skill is noticing which one the moment needs.

faqs.q: Is leadership only for senior or executive roles?
faqs.a: No. An individual contributor leads when they connect their work to the bigger goal, for example in a PR description, in how they frame a trade-off, or by raising a question the rest of the room would rather skip. Title and leadership behavior are only loosely related.

faqs.q: How do I add more leadership without hurting delivery?
faqs.a: Use small, repeated habits instead of a big initiative. Ask one what-or-why question for every three how-or-when questions, keep the goal visible where the team looks every day, write one line of why into each ticket, and now and then ask teammates to explain why their work matters.

faqs.q: What are the signs that a team is under-led?
faqs.a: The team is busy and organized and velocity looks fine, yet people can't say where the team is heading this quarter or why. Sprint goals read like ticket lists, trade-offs default to whatever is easiest this sprint, and strong engineers stop proposing ideas.
